chapters.desc: Before a student asks how to memorise, he must ask a more basic question: what do I need in order to learn at all? In four short abyāt, Shaykh Dr Waleed al-Meneese answers it. He does not give a study plan. He gives the conditions without which a study plan has nothing to stand on.

ajuzW.g: so here they are — take them
so that you gather it all

verses.tr: There are four conditions for knowledge; here they are, so take them all (and gather them with care).

exp.en:
The poet does not begin by telling us what knowledge is. He begins by telling us what knowledge requires.

شُرُوط Conditions

The word شُرُوط is the plural of شَرْط, a condition, requirement, or prerequisite. A sharṭ is something upon which the attainment or perfection of something else depends.

The poet therefore shifts our attention away from a modern question, “What can I learn?”, towards a far more important one: “What must I have in order to truly acquire knowledge?”

This matters in our time. A student can search for an explanation, watch a lecture, download a book or ask an AI a question within seconds. But access to information is not the same as acquiring knowledge.

The Prophet ﷺ described knowledge as a path:

مَنْ سَلَكَ طَرِيقًا يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْمًا سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقًا إِلَى الْجَنَّةِ

“Whoever treads a path seeking knowledge, Allah makes easy for him a path to Paradise.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

A path is not walked without provisions. The poet is handing the traveller his provisions before he sets out.

Even the Messenger ﷺ, the most knowledgeable of creation, was commanded to ask for more:

﴿وَقُلْ رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا﴾

“And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge.” Ṭā Hā 20:114

If the one who received revelation was told to seek increase, then no student may treat knowledge as something that simply arrives. It is sought, and it has conditions.

Why عِلْمٍ and not الْعِلْمِ?

The poet says شُرُوطُ عِلْمٍ, not شُرُوطُ الْعِلْمِ. The indefinite عِلْمٍ gives the expression breadth: the conditions for knowledge in general, not for one discipline. These principles apply across the student’s journey: Qurʾān, ḥadīth, fiqh, Arabic, tafsīr, qirāʾāt and every Islamic science.

أَرْبَعَةٌ Four

The poet tells us at once that there are four. This is characteristic of the scholarly tradition, where complex ideas are condensed into memorable structures. Instead of a long philosophical discussion about education, he gives the student four things to remember, and with them a framework for assessing himself: do I have the four?

فَهَاكَهَا “Here they are for you”

The فَـ connects the statement to what precedes it: “So here, then…”. And هَاكَ is an imperative meaning “Here, take this.” There is a sense of the teacher placing something into the student’s hands. That is exactly what happens in traditional learning: knowledge is received. The teacher has something to give, and the student must be prepared to take it.

لِتَجْمَعَهْ “So that you may gather them”

The poet does not say لِتَعْرِفَهَا, “so that you may know them.” He says لِتَجْمَعَهْ, “so that you may gather them.” It is not enough to know the four conditions. They must be brought together.

  • You can have a teacher but no books.
  • You can have excellent books but no teacher.
  • You can have both but lack consistency.
  • You can study consistently but have no system for preserving what you learn.

جَمْع versus مَعْرِفَة. Knowing the ingredients is not the same as putting them together. A student could memorise this entire poem and still fail to benefit if he never implements it.

There is a progression hidden inside the bayt: the poet tells you there are requirements, limits them to four, hands them to you, and then tells you what to do with them. A statement has become an instruction.

The principle behind the conditions

Before we examine the conditions one by one, there is a principle that governs the entire discussion:

إِنَّ هَذَا الْعِلْمَ دِينٌ، فَانْظُرُوا عَمَّنْ تَأْخُذُونَ دِينَكُمْ

“Indeed, this knowledge is religion, so look carefully from whom you take your religion.”

This is the famous statement of the great Tābiʿī Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ, recorded by Imām Muslim in the introduction to his Ṣaḥīḥ. It establishes a fundamental principle of the Islamic tradition: the person from whom we take knowledge matters.

Islamic knowledge is not merely information that we collect and store. It concerns what we believe, how we worship Allah, how we understand His Book, how we understand the Sunnah of His Messenger ﷺ, and ultimately how we live. For this reason, the student cannot treat every source as equal.

This is particularly important in our time. A person may have an impressive following, speak beautifully, produce polished videos, and appear constantly on social media, but none of these things establishes that he is qualified to teach the religion. The student therefore asks:

  • From whom did this person learn?
  • Who were his teachers?
  • What is his methodology?
  • Is he grounded in sound Islamic scholarship?
  • Is he known for honesty, integrity, and acting upon his knowledge?

Popularity is not scholarship, eloquence is not qualification, and visibility is not authority.

This is the meaning of Ibn Sīrīn’s instruction. And it is why it is so significant that, when the poet begins listing the conditions, the first thing he mentions is not a book, a course, or a technique. It is a teacher.

Perhaps this is where the poem begins to reveal its deeper message. The journey of knowledge is not simply about finding information. It is about finding the right people, the right sources, and the right habits through which knowledge can become firmly established.

Knowledge is not merely something you consume. It is something you cultivate. Before the poem teaches us what to study, it teaches us how to become the kind of person who can study.

verses.tr: A sincere (and guiding) Shaykh, and books that are sound, authentic, and beneficial.

exp.en:
The first condition is not a book. It is a teacher.

شَيْخٌ Why a teacher?

Allah describes the mission of His Messenger ﷺ in terms of teaching:

﴿هُوَ الَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي الْأُمِّيِّينَ رَسُولًا مِنْهُمْ يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آيَاتِهِ وَيُزَكِّيهِمْ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ الْكِتَابَ وَالْحِكْمَةَ وَإِنْ كَانُوا مِنْ قَبْلُ لَفِي ضَلَالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾

“It is He who sent among the unlettered a Messenger from among them, reciting to them His verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom.” al-Jumuʿah 62:2

The Book was not simply delivered to people as a text. It was recited, explained, and lived in front of them. Even Jibrīl عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ came to the Prophet ﷺ in the form of a man, and the Prophet ﷺ afterwards said: “He came to teach you your religion.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim And every Ramaḍān, Jibrīl would review the Qurʾān with the Prophet ﷺ. al-Bukhārī and Muslim

The Qurʾān also gives us a portrait of the ideal student. Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ, a Prophet of Allah, travelled to meet a servant of Allah who had been given knowledge he did not have, and he said:

﴿قَالَ لَهُ مُوسَىٰ هَلْ أَتَّبِعُكَ عَلَىٰ أَنْ تُعَلِّمَنِ مِمَّا عُلِّمْتَ رُشْدًا﴾

“May I follow you, so that you teach me of the right guidance you have been taught?” al-Kahf 18:66

Notice the humility of the request: may I follow you. The student does not summon the teacher. He goes to him.

The Qurʾān gives a general principle as well:

﴿فَاسْأَلُوا أَهْلَ الذِّكْرِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾

“So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know.” al-Naḥl 16:43

The early scholars understood that knowledge is a trust passed from person to person. This is why Ibn Sīrīn’s principle, discussed above, was repeated so often by the early scholars. And the Prophet ﷺ warned that knowledge disappears:

إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَقْبِضُ الْعِلْمَ انْتِزَاعًا يَنْتَزِعُهُ مِنَ الْعِبَادِ، وَلَكِنْ يَقْبِضُ الْعِلْمَ بِقَبْضِ الْعُلَمَاءِ

“Allah does not take knowledge away by snatching it from the people, but He takes knowledge by taking away the scholars.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

If knowledge leaves the world with its carriers, then it is also acquired through its carriers.

The teacher comes first because knowledge is not merely transferred from page to mind. Traditionally, it is transferred from teacher to student, from heart to heart, from one generation to the next. A sound teacher provides more than information. He provides direction, correction, context, and example. He teaches the student not only what to learn, but how to understand it, how to approach it and how to carry it. This is why the scholars were so concerned about who a student sat with.

The first condition is therefore not simply: find someone who knows. It is to find someone from whom knowledge can safely be taken.

نَصُوحٌ Not just any teacher

The poet does not say merely شَيْخٌ. He says شَيْخٌ نَصُوحٌ. The word نَصُوح is an intensive form of نَصَحَ, to give sincere counsel, and it describes someone whose sincerity in advising is deeply rooted.

The Prophet ﷺ said: الدِّينُ النَّصِيحَةُ, “Religion is sincere counsel.”

A teacher may be knowledgeable and still not be naṣūḥ. The sincere teacher wants good for his student. He corrects him without humiliating him, directs him to what is beneficial even when it is not what the student wants, and cares about his character as much as his recitation. This is the teacher of whom we will speak in the next poem: the one who gives a waṣiyyah and entrusts it to the student for his benefit.

This is also why the word “guiding” is apt. The Shaykh is not only a source of information. He is a guide. He knows what to teach, in what order, and when the student is ready.

كُتُبٌ صَحِيحَةٌ Sound books

Then the poet turns to books, and he qualifies them with two words. The first is صَحِيحَةٌ, sound and authentic. A book may be beautifully printed and still contain errors, weak reports, or distorted wording. Allah instructs the believers to verify:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِنْ جَاءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوا﴾

“O you who believe, if a wrongdoer brings you news, verify it.” al-Ḥujurāt 49:6

And the Prophet ﷺ warned: “Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim These warnings are why the scholars were so careful about the soundness of what they transmitted and what they wrote. This connects directly to ḍabṭ al-kitāb, the precision of the written record.

نَافِعَةٌ Beneficial

Not every sound book is the right book for this student at this stage. The Prophet ﷺ would seek refuge in Allah from knowledge that does not benefit:

اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ عِلْمٍ لَا يَنْفَعُ

“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit.” Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim

The student must therefore ask two questions of every book: is it reliable? And will it benefit me?

The poet places the teacher and the book side by side for a reason. A book without a teacher is exposed to misunderstanding, because the student has no one to correct his reading and understanding. Scholars have long warned that a student who takes knowledge from pages alone is prone to error. A teacher without books, on the other hand, leaves the student with nothing to return to, check, and revise. Each protects the other.

The teacher gives the book its voice, and the book gives the teacher’s words a home. Seek both and verify both.

verses.tr: Clear handwriting, and persist in studying them, and take along with it…

exp.en:
وُضُوحُ خَطٍّ Clear handwriting

This condition may surprise a modern reader. But the Qurʾān itself begins its revelation with the pen:

﴿اقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ الْأَكْرَمُ (٣) الَّذِي عَلَّمَ بِالْقَلَمِ (٤) عَلَّمَ الْإِنْسَانَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ (٥)﴾

“Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know.” al-ʿAlaq 96:3–5

Allah also swears by it:

﴿نٓ وَالْقَلَمِ وَمَا يَسْطُرُونَ﴾

“Nūn. By the pen and what they write.” al-Qalam 68:1

The Prophet ﷺ valued writing. When a man from Yemen asked for what he had heard in the Prophet’s sermon, the Prophet ﷺ said: اكْتُبُوا لِأَبِي شَاهٍ, “Write it down for Abū Shāh.” al-Bukhārī The Companions also said that knowledge should be bound by writing.

But the poet asks for more than writing. He asks for clear writing. Why? Because writing is memory’s insurance, and unclear writing is a broken policy.

A student who cannot read his own notes a month later has lost what he wrote. A smudged letter, a missing dot, or an ambiguous word can change a meaning, and in our sciences a single letter can change a ruling or a reading. Clear handwriting is therefore not vanity. It is ḍabṭ, the precise preservation of knowledge, on paper. It is the same concern for precision that guided the narrators of ḥadīth, now placed in the student’s own hand.

In our time the principle is wider than ink: whatever tools you use to record what you learn, make sure they are clear, organised and reviewable.

وَتُلِحْ فِي دَرْسِهَا Persist in studying

The verb تُلِحْ comes from أَلَحَّ, to insist, to be persistent and not let go. This is not casual study. It is persistence with insistence.

The Qurʾān gives us the example of Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ as he set out in search of knowledge:

﴿وَإِذْ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِفَتَاهُ لَا أَبْرَحُ حَتَّىٰ أَبْلُغَ مَجْمَعَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ أَوْ أَمْضِيَ حُقُبًا﴾

“I will not cease until I reach the meeting of the two seas, or I will continue for years.” al-Kahf 18:60

And Allah promises:

﴿وَالَّذِينَ جَاهَدُوا فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا﴾

“And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways.” al-ʿAnkabūt 29:69

Persistence in study is the engine that turns the other conditions into results.

The Prophet ﷺ taught the same principle in a way every student should remember:

أَحَبُّ الْأَعْمَالِ إِلَى اللَّهِ أَدْوَمُهَا وَإِنْ قَلَّ

“The most beloved of deeds to Allah are the most consistent, even if small.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

This echoes the heart of this book. Shaykh Waleed will later tell the memoriser to reduce the amount and maintain continuity. Here he tells the student of knowledge the same thing in different words.

وَخُذْ مَعَهْ “And take along with it”

The bayt ends with an open door. After the four conditions, the poet says: take along with them… and the next bayt completes the thought.

Write clearly so that nothing is lost. Study persistently so that nothing is forgotten. The pen preserves what the ear receives, and persistence preserves what the pen records.

verses.tr: A sound and discerning mind: some of them have added it and appended it.

exp.en:
The poet has said there are four conditions, and he has now named four: the teacher, the books, clear handwriting and persistence. But this final bayt tells us something about the people of knowledge: some of them added a further condition and appended it to the list. That addition is رَجَاحُ الْعَقْلِ, soundness of intellect. (The word is written رَجَاحَ here, evidently shortened from رَجَاحَةَ to suit the metre.)

The root رَجَحَ describes a scale that tips. A rājiḥ intellect is a weighty one: steady, balanced, able to weigh matters properly and reach the sound conclusion. It is not only brilliance. It is good judgement.

The Qurʾān repeatedly honours those who use their minds well. Allah says:

﴿يُؤْتِي الْحِكْمَةَ مَنْ يَشَاءُ ۚ وَمَنْ يُؤْتَ الْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا ۗ وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلَّا أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ﴾

“He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given much good. And none remember except those of understanding.” al-Baqarah 2:269

And the Prophet ﷺ said:

مَنْ يُرِدِ اللَّهُ بِهِ خَيْرًا يُفَقِّهْهُ فِي الدِّينِ

“Whoever Allah wants good for, He gives him understanding of the religion.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

Understanding is therefore a gift, and the poet reminds us it is something to ask for and to build.

In another well-known ḥadīth, the Prophet ﷺ prayed for those who convey knowledge and noted that perhaps the one to whom it is conveyed retains it better than the one who heard it. Retention and understanding are not limited to the first hearer. A sound mind can take what it is given and see more in it.

Why is this added, rather than counted?

There is a gentle wisdom in the structure. The four conditions can be acquired by effort: you can find a teacher, choose sound books, train your handwriting, and commit to persistence. Intellect is different. People are given different measures of it, which is why only “some” add it. By placing it as an addition rather than a fifth pillar, the poet avoids discouraging the student of ordinary ability. Whatever measure of intellect Allah has given you, you are told what to do with it: develop it.

And you develop it through the very conditions that came before. A sincere teacher trains the mind. Sound books feed it. The pen sharpens it, because to write something clearly, you must first understand it. And persistence strengthens it, as it strengthens any faculty that is used.

This also reminds us of what the book will teach throughout: the means are ours, but understanding is a gift. So the student asks Allah, as Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ did, to expand his chest and ease his affair, and he also uses the mind he has been given.

Do not wait to be given a better mind. Use the one you have, in the company of a sincere teacher, with sound books, a clear pen, and persistence, and ask the One who gives understanding to increase it.

Conclusion

The poem begins with conditions and ends with a mind. Along the way, it has told the student that knowledge is not a matter of access. It needs a person to learn from, a text to rely on, a pen to preserve it, and a will that does not let go. And it needs an intellect that weighs what it receives.

This connects to everything that follows. Ḥifẓ and ḍabṭ need the teacher who corrects and the book against which we check. Tathbīt needs persistence. And all of it, as the next six verses of poetry will teach us, is held in the hands of Allah, who gives tawfīq.

So take the four, gather them, add to them a mind that is trained and humble, and begin the journey: walking with the means in your hands and your heart with the One who makes the path easy.

The conditions for seeking knowledge

  • A sincere teacher شَيْخٌ نَصُوحٌ
    Protects direction, correct understanding and character.
  • Sound, beneficial books كُتُبٌ صَحِيحَةٌ وَنَافِعَةٌ
    Protect the reliability of what is learned.
  • Clear handwriting وُضُوحُ خَطٍّ
    Protects the preservation of what is learned.
  • Persistence وَتُلِحْ فِي دَرْسِهَا
    Protects continuity until knowledge is established.
  • Sound intellect (added by some) رَجَاحُ عَقْلٍ
    Protects understanding and good judgement.

chapters.en: Counsel for the One Who Memorises the Qurʾān
chapters.desc: Six abyāt built on the counsel of Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat, the Ḥanbalī jurist and teacher at the Prophet’s Mosque, for whoever seeks to master memorisation: reduce the amount, increase the repetition, keep at it, and hold fast to seeking forgiveness.

verses.tr: O you who seek memorisation, listen; may you be guided, and may you attain.

exp.en:
Before the poem

Shaykh Dr Waleed al-Meneese introduces the poem with these words:

أَعْجَبَتْنِي وَصِيَّةُ فَضِيلَةِ الشَّيْخِ الدُّكْتُورِ عَامِر بَهْجَتْ، الْفَقِيهِ الْحَنْبَلِيِّ الْمَعْرُوفِ، الْمُدَرِّسِ بِالْحَرَمِ النَّبَوِيِّ الشَّرِيفِ، لِمَنْ أَرَادَ إِتْقَانَ الْحِفْظِ، حَيْثُ قَالَ: «أَنْ تُقَلِّلَ الْمِقْدَارَ، وَتُكْثِرَ التِّكْرَارَ، وَتَحْرِصَ عَلَى الْمُدَاوَمَةِ وَالِاسْتِمْرَارِ، مَعَ مُلَازَمَةِ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ لِلْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ». فَنَظَمْتُ وَصِيَّتَهُ شِعْرًا، وَقُلْتُ نَصِيحَةً لِمَنْ يَحْفَظُ الْقُرْآنَ:

“I was struck by the counsel of His Eminence Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat, the well-known Ḥanbalī jurist who teaches at the Prophet’s Mosque, for whoever wishes to master memorisation, where he said: ‘Reduce the amount, increase the repetition, be diligent in maintaining consistency and continuity, while remaining constant in seeking forgiveness from the One, the All-Subduing.’ So I set his counsel in verse, and said, as advice for the one who memorises the Qurʾān:”

These few words address not only how much a student should memorise, but how he should repeat it, how he should sustain his efforts, and how he should maintain his relationship with Allah throughout the process. The poem can therefore be approached through four principles:

  1. تَقْلِيلُ الْمِقْدَارِ Take less, but master it. Resist the temptation to measure progress by quantity. The aim is not to see how much can be taken in at once. The aim is to establish what is taken. Less, but better.
  2. كَثْرَةُ التِّكْرَارِ Repeat until it settles. What is repeated receives another opportunity to become established. The student does not repeat because he has failed to memorise. He repeats because repetition is part of memorisation itself.
  3. الْمُدَاوَمَةُ وَالِاسْتِمْرَارُ Consistency over intensity. There is a difference between a learner who occasionally memorises a great deal and one who consistently memorises a little. The first may experience bursts of progress. The second builds permanence. Consistency is itself a method of mastery.
  4. مُلَازَمَةُ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ Learning with Allah. The final principle takes the discussion beyond technique. The student works, repeats, revises, and perseveres. Yet he recognises that the opening of the heart, the strength of memory and the ability to establish knowledge are ultimately gifts from Allah.

The first bayt

The poem begins with a direct address. Shaykh Waleed does not begin by giving the student a technique, a schedule, or several pages to memorise. He begins by speaking to the person himself:

يَا مَنْ يَرُومُ الْحِفْظَا “O you who seek memorisation”

There is something deliberate in the choice of the verb رَامَ. The Arabs use رَامَ for one who seeks, pursues or aspires to something with intention. It is more purposeful than simply wanting something. There is movement in the word. The person who يَرُومُ something has set his heart upon it and is pursuing it.

The student must first want to memorise, but not merely desire the result. He must become a seeker of it. There is a difference between saying, “I wish I could memorise this,” and deciding, “I am going to pursue its memorisation.” The first is a wish; the second is a journey.

This is where the journey begins: with aspiration.

اسْمَعْ Listen

It is striking that before he tells the student how to memorise, he tells him to listen. The first instruction is not write, read, repeat or even memorise. It is listen.

This reminds us that learning begins with reception. A student who does not know how to listen will struggle to know how to learn. The ear is often the first doorway through which knowledge enters, and what we repeatedly hear has a remarkable ability to settle within us.

Repetition does something to the mind. What we repeatedly encounter becomes familiar. What becomes familiar becomes easier to recall. And what we continually engage with can eventually become so firmly established that we recite it almost without conscious effort. There is, however, another side to this principle that every student should consider carefully.

Memorisation, then, is not a single event. It is a relationship of continual engagement.

If repetition teaches the mind, then we must ask ourselves what we are repeatedly teaching it. We are often careful about what we deliberately memorise, but much less careful about what we repeatedly listen to.

A person may say, “I never intended to memorise this song,” yet after hearing it dozens of times, he knows every word. A phrase from a video, a line from a film, a jingle from an advertisement, or even a piece of casual conversation can become lodged in the memory simply because it has been repeated often enough.

The mind does not always ask whether what it is receiving is worthy of being remembered. Repetition itself leaves an impression. Be careful what you repeatedly expose your ears to, because you may be memorising without realising that you are memorising.

This gives the word اسْمَعْ an additional dimension. The student of knowledge must learn not only how to listen, but what to listen to.

This is one reason why the Islamic tradition placed such emphasis upon the company of scholars, the recitation of Qurʾān, the repeated study of texts and the constant revisiting of beneficial knowledge. The learner’s environment matters because repeated exposure shapes the contents of the mind.

هُدِيتَ May you be guided

The phrase is beautiful because a supplication is embedded within the instruction. He does not merely command the student to listen. He asks Allah to guide him.

There is a subtle lesson here. The acquisition of knowledge is not simply an intellectual process. A person may possess information without possessing guidance. He may memorise words without understanding their purpose. He may retain a text without allowing the text to transform him. The student therefore needs هِدَايَة. He needs Allah to guide him to what he should learn, to whom he should learn from, to how he should learn it, and ultimately to how he should live by what he has learned.

تُحْظَى May you attain

The word comes from حَظِيَ, which carries the meaning of attaining something desirable, receiving favour, or being fortunate enough to obtain a benefit. So the four movements of the verse are striking:

تَرُومُ ← اسْمَعْ ← هُدِيتَ ← تُحْظَى

You aspire → you listen → you seek guidance → you attain.

The order matters because the student does not simply leap from desire to achievement. There is a process between the two. Aspiration must be followed by receptiveness, and receptiveness must be accompanied by guidance.

This also teaches us something about the nature of mastery. We often look at someone who has memorised a great amount and see only the result. We do not see the thousands of small acts of listening, repetition, revision and persistence that produced it.

The first bayt therefore establishes the character of the memoriser before it gives us the method of memorisation. Before asking, “How much should I memorise?”, ask: “What am I seeking?” Before asking, “How many times should I repeat?”, ask: “What am I allowing myself to repeatedly hear?” And before trusting your own ability, ask Allah for هِدَايَة.

What you repeatedly hear, you may eventually remember; therefore, be deliberate about what you allow to become familiar to your mind and heart.

sadrW.g: of Ibn Bahjat (Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat)

verses.tr: This is the counsel of Ibn Bahjat, intended for the one who understands it and firmly establishes it.

exp.en:
The first bayt addressed the seeker directly:

يَا مَنْ يَرُومُ الْحِفْظَا

“O you who seek memorisation.”

Now, in the second bayt, Shaykh Waleed introduces the source of the advice.

وَصِيَّةَ ابْنِ بَهْجَتْ “The counsel of Ibn Bahjat”

The word وَصِيَّة deserves our attention. A waṣiyyah is not simply a casual suggestion or an interesting piece of information. It is counsel given with concern for the one who receives it, something entrusted to another for his benefit.

The Qurʾān repeatedly uses the language of waṣiyyah and tawāṣī when speaking about matters of importance. Allah says:

﴿وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْحَقِّ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ﴾

“And they counsel one another with truth, and they counsel one another with patience.” al-ʿAṣr 103:3

The expression تَوَاصَوْا is particularly beautiful because it describes something more than one person simply giving advice. It suggests a community in which beneficial counsel is continually passed from one person to another. One receives it, benefits from it, and then becomes part of its transmission. That is precisely what we see in these verses.

Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat offered this counsel concerning the mastery of memorisation. Shaykh Dr Waleed Idris al-Meneese encountered those words, recognised their value, and did not allow them to remain merely something he had heard. He remembered them, understood them, preserved them, and then transformed them into poetry. There is something remarkable in that transformation. He did not merely repeat the advice. He made it easier for others to repeat. He took a valuable piece of counsel and placed it into a form that could itself be memorised. In doing so, the advice travelled another step along the chain of knowledge:

سَمِعَ ← وَعَى ← حَفِظَ ← نَظَمَ ← بَلَّغَ

He heard → understood → retained → composed → transmitted.

This is, in many ways, the very process that the poem itself teaches.

This gives the word وَصِيَّة another layer of meaning for us as students. When a teacher gives advice, perhaps the responsibility of the student is not simply to say, “I have heard it.” The student should ask: have I understood it? Then: have I preserved it? And eventually: how can I pass its benefit to someone else? This is the spirit of scholarly transmission.

لِمَنْ وَعَى For the one who understands and retains

The choice of وَعَى is particularly powerful. The word carries meanings of understanding, comprehending, retaining, and holding something firmly within oneself. Allah says:

﴿لِنَجْعَلَهَا لَكُمْ تَذْكِرَةً وَتَعِيَهَا أُذُنٌ وَاعِيَةٌ﴾

“So that We may make it a reminder for you, and that a receptive ear may retain it.” al-Ḥāqqah 69:12

Notice the connection between this verse and the first bayt. There we were told اسْمَعْ: listen. Now we are told وَعَى: understand and retain. The ear hears, but the mind must comprehend, and the heart must receive. Hearing alone is not learning.

But Shaykh Waleed does not stop at وَعَى.

وَثَبَّتْ And firmly establishes

From ثَبَّتَ, meaning to make something firm, establish it, strengthen it, and cause it to remain.

This takes us from acquisition to preservation. The student does not merely want to have encountered the information. He wants it to become firmly established. This is the most important distinction for anyone studying the Qurʾān or a text: الْحِفْظُ is not the end. There is التَّثْبِيتُ.

The challenge is not simply to place the Qurʾān into one’s memory. It is to continually strengthen what has been placed there.

You may memorise a page today, but the real question is whether that page will still be with you next month, next year, and many years from now. This is why the advice of Ibn Bahjat is so relevant to the ḥāfiẓ.

The same principle is evident in the story of this very poem. Shaykh Dr Waleed did not simply hear the advice of Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat and move on. He ثَبَّتَ it: he preserved it, reflected upon it, and then gave it another form so that others could preserve it too. The student who receives knowledge should aspire to become a link in that chain.

He should not merely ask, “What can I memorise?” but, “What can I preserve well enough that I can pass it on?”

That is the difference between collecting knowledge and carrying knowledge. This is why the word وَصِيَّة is so appropriate. A waṣiyyah is something entrusted to you. You are not its destination. You are a trustee in the chain.

The true student does not allow beneficial knowledge to end with him; he receives it with understanding, preserves it with care, and passes it on in a form others can carry.

verses.tr: Reduce the amount, and increase the repetition.

exp.en:
With this bayt, Shaykh Waleed moves from describing the character of the seeker to giving him his first practical principle.

The advice is remarkably simple: take less, repeat more. Yet behind these few words lies one of the most important principles in the entire science of memorisation.

أَنْ قَلِّلِ الْمِقْدَارَا Reduce the amount

The verb قَلِّلْ comes from قَلَّلَ, meaning to reduce, lessen, or make something smaller. The goal remains memorisation. What changes is the portion being taken at one time.

The learner may naturally assume that progress is measured by quantity. If one page is good, perhaps two pages are better. If ten verses can be memorised today, perhaps twenty would represent even greater progress. But Shaykh Waleed reverses that instinct.

The question is not simply: how much did I cover? The better question is: how firmly did what I covered become established?

This principle has a powerful precedent in the way the Companions رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمْ learned the Qurʾān. It is reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ that the Companions would learn ten verses from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they would not move beyond them until they had learned what was contained in them in terms of knowledge and action. He said:

كَانَ الرَّجُلُ مِنَّا إِذَا تَعَلَّمَ عَشْرَ آيَاتٍ لَمْ يُجَاوِزْهُنَّ حَتَّى يَعْرِفَ مَعَانِيَهُنَّ وَالْعَمَلَ بِهِنَّ

“When a man among us learned ten verses, he would not move beyond them until he had understood their meanings and acted upon them.”

This report presents a profoundly different conception of learning. The objective was not simply to finish ten verses so that another ten could be added. The verses were allowed to settle. They were learned, understood, acted upon, and only then did the learner proceed.

This gives us an important dimension to the word مِقْدَار. The portion of knowledge given to a student should be small enough that he can do justice to it. The Companions were not merely collecting verses. They were allowing the Qurʾān to become knowledge, understanding, and action.

Reducing the amount does not necessarily mean reducing progress. Sometimes, taking less allows you to absorb more.

A student who memorises twenty verses but struggles to recall them a week later may have covered more ground than the student who memorised ten verses and retained them firmly. But if the second student understands them, acts upon them and can still recall them months later, who has truly progressed further? The answer depends on how we define progress. If progress means covering pages, the first student appears ahead. If progress means establishing knowledge, the picture changes completely.

وَكَثِّرِ التِّكْرَارَا Increase the repetition

Now Shaykh Waleed gives us the other half of the equation, and the contrast is deliberate:

أَنْ قَلِّلِ الْمِقْدَارَا ۞ وَكَثِّرِ التِّكْرَارَا

“Reduce the amount, and increase the repetition.”

The student is not being told to reduce his effort. He is being told to redistribute his effort. Take a smaller amount and then give that amount more attention. Read it, recall it without looking, return to it, test yourself, recite it again, then return to it tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that.

This is why repetition is not a sign that the student is struggling. Repetition is the method. The Prophet ﷺ himself emphasised the need to continually engage with the Qurʾān. He said:

“Keep reviewing this Qurʾān, for by the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Muhammad, it escapes more quickly than camels from their ropes.” al-Bukhārī and Muslim

The image is powerful. A camel tied by its rope does not remain secure simply because it was tied yesterday. It requires attention. If it is neglected, it may escape. Likewise, memorisation requires continual engagement.

The student who says, “I already know this, let me move on,” may be moving away from the very practice that makes his knowledge firm. There is a difference between recognising something and being able to retrieve it. Something may look familiar when the page is open yet disappear when the book is closed.

Repetition helps move knowledge beyond familiarity towards reliable recall.

This is also why the Qurʾān speaks about gradual revelation:

﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَوْلَا نُزِّلَ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ جُمْلَةً وَاحِدَةً ۚ كَذَٰلِكَ لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤَادَكَ ۖ وَرَتَّلْنَاهُ تَرْتِيلًا﴾

“And those who disbelieved said, ‘Why was the Qurʾān not revealed to him all at once?’ Thus, so that We may strengthen your heart with it, and We have revealed it with measured recitation.” al-Furqān 25:32

Allah connects the gradual revelation of the Qurʾān with لِنُثَبِّتَ بِهِ فُؤَادَكَ, “so that We may strengthen your heart with it.”

There is therefore a profound lesson in allowing knowledge to arrive gradually and to be revisited repeatedly. Less can become more. This is where the advice of Ibn Bahjat becomes particularly relevant to modern students. We live in an age of abundance. Information is everywhere. Students can access lectures, books, podcasts, videos, courses, and articles within seconds. The temptation is therefore to consume more and more. But consumption is not the same as learning. A student can watch ten lectures and remember very little. Another can study one principle deeply, repeat it, explain it to someone else, apply it, and revisit it until it becomes part of his intellectual framework. The second student may have consumed less, but he may have learned more.

Do not measure learning by how much entered your mind, but by how much remained there and changed you.

This is the wisdom behind قَلِّلِ الْمِقْدَارَ، وَكَثِّرِ التِّكْرَارَ. The goal of learning is not to move quickly through knowledge, but to allow knowledge to move deeply into you. Or, as a question for the student: would you rather finish more today, or remember more tomorrow? That is the tension Shaykh Waleed places before us.

Reduce what you take in so that you can increase what you do with it. This is the principle we should carry into every aspect of learning.

verses.tr: Maintain continuity, and remain committed to seeking forgiveness.

exp.en:
The first two bayts established the seeker’s character, and the third gave him his first method: do not chase quantity; chase quality, التَّثْبِيت. With this bayt, Shaykh Waleed adds two things that every serious student needs: consistency in effort and consistency in returning to Allah.

وَأَدِمِ اسْتِمْرَارَا Maintain continuity

The word أَدِمْ comes from أَدَامَ, meaning to maintain something, continue it, preserve it, and make it last. Then comes اسْتِمْرَارَا, from اسْتَمَرَّ, meaning to continue, persist and carry on. There is therefore a beautiful reinforcement in the wording, أَدِمِ اسْتِمْرَارَا, almost as though he is saying: “Continue continuing.”

The message could hardly be clearer: do not merely begin well. Continue.

This is particularly important in memorisation because the greatest obstacle is not always inability. Very often, it is inconsistency. A student may have an extraordinary day: “Today I memorised three pages!” But memorisation is not ultimately measured by what we can achieve on our best day. It is measured by what we can sustain.

What can you repeat tomorrow? What can you maintain next week? What can you continue when the excitement has disappeared? This takes us directly back to the previous bayt: قَلِّلِ الْمِقْدَارَا, reduce the amount. Why? Because a manageable amount is more likely to be sustained. There is a beautiful relationship between the two instructions:

قَلِّلِ الْمِقْدَارَ ← أَدِمِ الِاسْتِمْرَارَ

Reduce the amount so that you can continue.

The student who attempts too much may make impressive progress for a few days and then stop altogether. The student who takes a smaller portion may appear slower, but if he continues for months and years, his accumulated progress can become extraordinary. Consistency turns small actions into substantial achievement.

وَالْتَزِمِ اسْتِغْفَارَا Commit yourself to seeking forgiveness

Then comes something that may initially seem unexpected. Notice that Shaykh Waleed does not simply say وَاسْتَغْفِرْ, “seek forgiveness.” He says وَالْتَزِمِ اسْتِغْفَارَا: make istighfār something to which you adhere. The verb الْتَزَمَ carries the meaning of adhering to something, committing oneself to it, and holding firmly to it. Istighfār therefore becomes part of the student’s way of life, not an occasional phrase uttered only when something goes wrong. Here the poem takes us beyond technique.

The previous bayt taught us الْمِقْدَارُ وَالتِّكْرَارُ: quantity and repetition. This bayt adds الِاسْتِمْرَارُ وَالِاسْتِغْفَارُ: consistency and seeking forgiveness.

The student is being taught to take the means while recognising the One who grants success through those means. You reduce your portion, repeat, and remain consistent. But you do not imagine that your memory, intelligence, or discipline is sufficient by itself. You ask Allah for tawfīq.

Why istighfār?

Allah Himself connects seeking forgiveness with opening doors and granting increase. Nūḥ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ said to his people:

﴿فَقُلْتُ اسْتَغْفِرُوا رَبَّكُمْ إِنَّهُ كَانَ غَفَّارًا (١٠) يُرْسِلِ السَّمَاءَ عَلَيْكُمْ مِدْرَارًا (١١) وَيُمْدِدْكُمْ بِأَمْوَالٍ وَبَنِينَ وَيَجْعَلْ لَكُمْ جَنَّاتٍ وَيَجْعَلْ لَكُمْ أَنْهَارًا (١٢)﴾

“I said, ‘Seek forgiveness from your Lord; indeed, He is ever Most Forgiving. He will send down upon you abundant rain, give you increase in wealth and children, provide you with gardens, and provide you with rivers.’” Nūḥ 71:10–12

Istighfār is therefore not merely an expression of regret. It is an act of returning to Allah. The student wants an increase in knowledge, but before becoming preoccupied with increasing what he possesses, he learns to ask Allah to forgive what stands between him and benefit.

Knowledge is not merely information deposited into the mind. It is a light and a gift from Allah, and the student approaches it with humility, repentance, and dependence upon Him.

This is where the Islamic understanding of knowledge differs from a purely technical model of learning. It also brings us to a subject that the tradition of Islamic scholarship has never treated lightly: the relationship between sin and the ability to benefit from knowledge.

It would be too simplistic to speak about sin as though every lapse automatically causes a measurable neurological decline in memory. Rather, the Islamic tradition speaks about something deeper: the effect of sin upon the heart, upon one’s receptivity to knowledge, and upon the tawfīq of Allah.

A student may spend hours trying to strengthen his memory while neglecting the state of the heart that is supposed to carry what he memorises. This is why the scholars frequently connected the pursuit of knowledge with taqwā, sincerity, repentance, and the avoidance of disobedience.

The memoriser should therefore examine not only his revision schedule, but also his relationship with Allah. When memorisation becomes difficult, we naturally ask: “How many times should I repeat this?” That is a good question. But perhaps we should sometimes ask another: “What is the state of the heart with which I am trying to carry this knowledge?”

This does not mean that every weakness in memory is the result of sin. Human beings forget. Fatigue, stress, age, distraction, and countless other factors affect our ability to remember. Nor should a student become trapped in guilt every time he struggles to recall something. Rather, istighfār teaches us humility. We take the practical means while continually returning to Allah.

The architecture is becoming clearer

Look at the progression of the first four bayts:

الرَّغْبَةُ ← السَّمَاعُ ← الْوَعْيُ ← التَّثْبِيتُ ← تَقْلِيلُ الْمِقْدَارِ ← كَثْرَةُ التِّكْرَارِ ← الِاسْتِمْرَارُ ← الِاسْتِغْفَارُ

Aspiration → listening → understanding → consolidation → manageable quantity → repetition → consistency → seeking forgiveness.

The student has now been given much more than a memorisation technique. He has been given a way of approaching knowledge. Take a manageable amount, repeat it, make it firm, continue, and throughout the entire process, return to Allah.

Take the means as though the work depends upon you, and turn to Allah knowing that success was never in your hands to begin with.

verses.tr: Ask Allah, the All-Subduing, whether in private or aloud.

exp.en:
With this bayt, Shaykh Waleed brings the practical journey of memorisation back to its spiritual foundation. The student has been told to reduce his portion, increase his repetition, remain consistent, and commit himself to istighfār. But after all these instructions comes one command.

وَلْتَسْأَلِ الْقَهَّارَا Ask the All-Subduing

It is as though the poet is reminding us: you have been given the means, but never forget the One who gives you the ability to benefit from them.

The word الْقَهَّار is one of the Names of Allah. It comes from the root ق ه ر, which carries the meanings of overpowering, subduing, conquering, and having complete dominion. Allah says:

﴿قُلِ اللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَهُوَ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ﴾

“Say: Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the All-Subduing.” al-Raʿd 13:16

Why this particular Name?

Because the memoriser is being reminded of something that is easy to forget: there are things in this journey that are beyond his control. You can choose your portion, organise your schedule, repeat a passage ten times, twenty times, or a hundred times, revise in the morning, and revise again at night. But you cannot command your heart to understand. You cannot force your mind to retain. You cannot guarantee that you will remember something tomorrow simply because you remembered it today. The ability to understand, retain, recall, and benefit is ultimately from Allah.

Sometimes a passage seems impossible. You repeat it again and again, and it refuses to settle. Then, by Allah’s permission, something changes. The words suddenly become familiar. The verses begin to flow. What seemed difficult becomes easy. The means were taken, but the tawfīq came from Allah. That is why the student turns to الْقَهَّار: the One whose power is absolute, the One who controls what we cannot control.

فِي السِّرِّ أَوْ جِهَارَا Whether secretly or openly

The contrast is beautiful. السِّرّ is what is hidden and private. الْجَهْر is what is expressed openly and audibly.

The student is therefore encouraged to ask Allah in every circumstance. When you are alone with your Qurʾān, ask Him. When you are sitting before your teacher, ask Him. When you are walking to class, ask Him. When a passage refuses to stay in your memory, ask Him. And when memorisation is flowing effortlessly, ask Him then too. Do not allow duʿāʾ to become something you only remember when you are struggling. The relationship with Allah accompanies the entire journey.

There is also a beautiful connection between this bayt and the one immediately before it. Shaykh Waleed said وَالْتَزِمِ اسْتِغْفَارَا, “commit yourself to istighfār”, and then وَلْتَسْأَلِ الْقَهَّارَا, “ask the All-Subduing.” The memoriser is therefore given two spiritual tools:

الِاسْتِغْفَارُ وَالِاسْتِعَانَةُ Seeking forgiveness and seeking assistance

The first turns the heart away from reliance upon one’s own perfection. The second turns it towards reliance upon Allah’s power. This is the spiritual psychology of the student of knowledge. Take the means, but do not worship the means.

Istighfār reminds the student: I am deficient. Duʿāʾ reminds him: Allah is able.

This is an extraordinarily balanced approach. Islam does not teach the student to abandon the means and simply wait for divine assistance. Nor does it teach him to become so dependent upon the methods that he forgets Allah. Take the means with diligence and seek the result from Allah.

  • You revise, but Allah grants retention.
  • You study, but Allah grants understanding.
  • You repeat, but Allah makes the knowledge firm.
  • You strive, but Allah grants tawfīq.

This is why the journey of memorisation can become an act of worship. Every repetition can be an act of obedience. Every struggle can become an opportunity for patience. Every successful recall can remind you of the One who made it possible. Allah says:

﴿وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ادْعُونِي أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ﴾

“And your Lord said: Call upon Me; I will respond to you.” Ghāfir 40:60

And He says:

﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ ۖ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ﴾

“When My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me.” al-Baqarah 2:186

The student is therefore never truly alone in the process. There is a teacher, books, methods, repetition and discipline, but above all, there is Allah.

Work until your effort is exhausted, then remember that the result was never yours to command.
Take every means available to you, but let your heart remain attached to the One who gives the means their effect.

verses.tr: [Ask Him for] assistance and support, success and felicity.

exp.en:
Shaykh Waleed has now taken the student from the instruction to ask Allah to what he should ask Him for. And the four words he chooses are carefully arranged:

الْعَوْنُ ← الْإِمْدَادُ ← الْفَوْزُ ← الْإِسْعَادُ

Assistance → reinforcement → success → felicity.

الْعَوْنَ Assistance

The word الْعَوْن carries the meaning of help, assistance, and support in accomplishing something. There is an important distinction here. The student is not asking Allah to do the work instead of him. He is asking Allah to help him while he does the work. There is a difference between “O Allah, memorise this for me” and “O Allah, help me to memorise it.”

The first imagines divine assistance as a replacement for human effort. The second recognises divine assistance as the very thing that allows human effort to bear fruit. This is beautifully captured in the language of الْعَوْن. The student is already striving, sitting with the Qurʾān or text, repeating, revising, struggling, and doing what he can. And then he says: يَا اللَّهُ، أَعِنِّي, “O Allah, help me.”

الْعَوْن is not a substitute for effort

This is one of the most important lessons for the memoriser. Some people understand tawakkul incorrectly. They imagine that relying upon Allah means doing nothing and simply waiting for Allah to provide the result. But that is not the Qurʾānic model.

We take the means because Allah commanded us to take them, while recognising that the means themselves only produce results by His permission. This is why we recite every day:

﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾

“You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help.” al-Fātiḥah 1:5

Notice the order: نَعْبُدُ, we worship; then نَسْتَعِينُ, we seek help. There is action before the request for assistance.

We worship, we strive, we take the means. And while doing so, we recognise that we cannot accomplish anything without Allah. The student therefore does not say, “I will ask Allah, so I don’t need to work.” Rather, he says, “I will work to the best of my ability, and I will ask Allah to make my effort fruitful.” That is الِاسْتِعَانَة.

الْعَوْن and النَّصْر

There is also a useful distinction between الْعَوْن and النَّصْر. النَّصْر is generally associated with victory, overcoming opposition, and being granted triumph over an adversary or difficulty. But الْعَوْن is broader. It is assistance given to a person as he undertakes an action.

A student does not necessarily need to be “defeating” something to need عَوْن, nor is he standing at the end of the road asking Allah to carry him there. He is walking the road and asking Allah to help him walk it well.

وَالْإِمْدَادَا Reinforcement and continued support

The word الْإِمْدَاد comes from أَمَدَّ, carrying the meaning of supplying, providing, reinforcing and furnishing someone with what he needs. There is therefore a subtle difference between the two:

  • الْعَوْن: help me in what I am doing.
  • الْإِمْدَاد: continue supplying me with what I need to keep doing it.

The memoriser needs both. He needs help to begin; then he needs continued support to persist. He needs strength today, and he needs strength tomorrow. He needs clarity when learning, and firmness when revising. He needs motivation when beginning, and مَدَد when the excitement has disappeared. This is why the combination is so beautiful.

الْعَوْنَ وَالْإِمْدَادَ: “Help me, and continue to supply me with what I need.”

وَالْفَوْزَ Success

Then the poem moves from the means to the outcome. The Qurʾān gives the word فَوْز a much greater meaning than simply accomplishing a worldly objective. Allah says:

﴿فَمَنْ زُحْزِحَ عَنِ النَّارِ وَأُدْخِلَ الْجَنَّةَ فَقَدْ فَازَ﴾

“Whoever is kept away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has certainly attained success.” Āl ʿImrān 3:185

This is the فَوْز that ultimately matters. The student may begin this journey thinking, “I want to memorise the Qurʾān.” That is a noble goal. But the poem teaches him to raise his aspiration. Do not merely ask Allah to help you finish. Ask Him to make what you memorise a means of true success, because it is possible to memorise something without allowing it to transform you.

The real question is not merely, “How much Qurʾān is in my memory?” but, “How much of the Qurʾān is visible in my life?”

وَالْإِسْعَادَا Felicity

From أَسْعَدَ, to bring happiness, felicity, and good fortune. This is a beautiful way for the poem to conclude. The student is not merely asking for achievement. He is asking for the good that should flow from achievement. Knowledge should bring him closer to Allah. Memorisation should strengthen his relationship with the Qurʾān. The Qurʾān should shape his character. That should ultimately become a source of سَعَادَة in this world and the next.

A complete spiritual formula

Now look at the last two verses together:

  • Whom should you ask? وَلْتَسْأَلِ الْقَهَّارَا
  • When should you ask? فِي السِّرِّ أَوْ جِهَارَا
  • What should you ask for along the journey? الْعَوْنَ وَالْإِمْدَادَا
  • And what should you ultimately seek? وَالْفَوْزَ وَالْإِسْعَادَا

The answers are beautifully structured, and now the whole poem begins to read less like a collection of memorisation tips and more like a spiritual methodology for the student of knowledge:

  1. Reduce the amount.
  2. Increase the repetition.
  3. Remain consistent.
  4. Seek forgiveness.
  5. Ask Allah.
  6. Seek His assistance.
  7. Seek His continued support.
  8. Ask Him to make the journey a means of true success and felicity.

There is something particularly important here for our age. We have become very good at developing systems, study plans, revision schedules, spaced repetition, memory techniques, productivity methods and digital tools, and all of these may be beneficial. But the believer understands that methodology is a means, not a deity.

We do not abandon the means. We perfect them. But we do not place our hearts in them. We place our hearts with Allah. That is why the memoriser can say, “I will repeat this verse as many times as necessary,” and at the same time: إِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ, You alone we ask for help.

He works with his hands, his tongue, and his mind, while his heart remains dependent upon Allah. That is not laziness. That is ʿubūdiyyah.

Tie the rope, repeat the verse, take every means you can; then raise your heart to Allah, for effort is yours, but tawfīq is His.

Conclusion

Six abyāt, and an entire methodology has unfolded before us. What began as a few lines of counsel from Shaykh Dr ʿĀmir Bahjat, versified by Shaykh Dr Waleed Idris al-Meneese, has revealed itself to be a complete framework for the student of knowledge: not merely a set of memorisation techniques, but a way of approaching the Qurʾān, the sciences of the Sharīʿah and knowledge itself.

The journey moved from character to method, and from method to the heart. The student was first addressed as a seeker: one who aspires, who listens, who is guided and who attains. He was then handed a waṣiyyah, counsel entrusted to him, for the one who understands it and firmly establishes it. From there came the practical principles: reduce the amount and increase the repetition; maintain continuity and remain committed to seeking forgiveness. And finally, the poem lifted the student’s gaze beyond technique altogether, teaching him to ask Allah, the All-Subduing, for assistance, reinforcement, success and felicity.

At every stage, the manẓūmah refused to separate the mechanical from the spiritual. The student is taught to take the means: to reduce his portion, to repeat it, to remain consistent, exactly as ḍabṭ demanded of the narrators of ḥadīth and as tathbīt demanded of every ḥāfiẓ who wished not merely to memorise the Qurʾān but to retain it. Yet at every stage, he is also taught that the means do not act by themselves. Effort is his; tawfīq is Allah’s.

This balance is, in the end, the greatest lesson of the poem. It would have been easy for Shaykh Waleed to leave us with a purely technical formula: reduce, repeat, persist. Many books on learning offer exactly that, and their advice is not without value. But the manẓūmah insists on something more. It insists that the heart with which a person memorises matters as much as the method by which he memorises. Istighfār and duʿāʾ are not appended to the method as an afterthought; they are woven into it as its final and necessary ingredients.

I ask Allah to accept this small effort, to forgive its shortcomings, and to make it of benefit to every ḥāfiẓ, every student and every teacher who reads it. May He grant us the ability to reduce our portion and increase our repetition, to remain consistent in our effort and constant in seeking His forgiveness, and to ask Him, in private and in public, for His assistance, His continued support, and ultimately, true success and felicity in this life and the next.

Take less, repeat more, remain constant, and let every act of memorisation be joined to an act of turning back to Allah, for the chest that carries knowledge well is the chest that has first been humbled before its Giver.

وَاللَّهُ وَلِيُّ التَّوْفِيقِ
